newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW-Russia GDP to dip again, reformer says.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Russia GDP to dip again, reformer says.

text.p: Russia's "vague political situation" and dearth of economic reforms will cause the nation's economy to decline again in 1997, key Russian reformer and economist Grigory Yavlinsky, forecast on Tuesday.
"The government should do real reforms and it is like paralyzed. It is doing nothing" to spur the economy, Yavlinsky told Reuters in an interview Tuesday at a New York hotel.
He said outdated thinking was hindering Russia President Boris Yeltsin from solving Russia's economic problems.

Yavlinsky, a high-profile politician who finished fourth in the 1996 presidential elections. predicted Russia's economy would decline in 1997 at the same pace it contracted in 1996. He said he expects gross domestic product (GDP) to fall by six percent, while industrial output drops about eight percent and overall capital investment falls 18 percent.
Yavlinsky sprang to prominence as the author of a 1990 plan to reform the economy in 500 days. He now leads the reform-minded Yabloko party holding about one-tenth of the Duma's seats.
In the interview, he blamed powerful "semi-criminal oligopolistic and overly monopolistic" forces in Russia as a major obstacle to reforms.
"It is necessary to make some concrete things, like competition, like demonopolization, like free trade, like land reform," he said.
"We have to overcome a very dangerous stage not to become semi-criminal, oligarchic and monpolistic state, which we are now just becoming," he said.
Yavlinsky was in New York to talk to investors on a trip sponsored by the Brunswick Brokerage firm, which specializes in Russia.
He said his gloomy 1997 outlook was based on several political factors.

"The political situation is very vague because Yeltsin is very unstable," he said. He stressed that he was referring to Yeltsin's inability to turn around the economy and introduce political reforms, not his physical health.
"His sickness is not a mental sickness ... he can stay on in the office" he said.

In Moscow, an alert-looking Yeltsin appeared Tuesday on Russian television for the first time in three weeks in a bid to calm concerns about his long-term health. In recent months he underwent a heart operation and a bout with pneumonia.
Yavlinsky said Yeltsin's problem was not his health but his outdated mentality.
"(Yeltsin's) time has passed two or three years ago because he is not prepared just now to solve any single problem in Russia."
"He can't identify the task, he can't find a way of solving the task and he can't find the people ... to solve it."
Yavlinsky said Yeltsin missed an opportunity to introduce wide-scale reform just after his re-election in June 1996, when he enjoyed a wide mandate and was strong politically.
"He didn't do anything new, he didn't change, he is continuing to rule Russia like Byzantium ... he is perfectly strong in intrigue."
Even so, Yavlinsky last week opposed an attempt to impeach Yeltsin. In the interview, he cited two reasons for wanting Yeltsin to stay in office until the end of his term.

Yeltsin, being the choice of the people, should under democratic principles, remain in the office until his term ends. In addition, Yavlinsky said there was a potential danger of allowing anyone to become president under the current constitution, which he termed "authoritarian" because it overly centralized power to that position.

As it stood, he said the president had excessively wide powers. "He can wake up in the morning, drink a cup of coffee and order a war, which kills 100,000 people," he said in an allusion to the death toll in the Chechnya war.
His party Yabloko had begun negotiations to revamp the constitution to narrow presidential powers and decentralize authority to local regions below the level of governor.
Outlining his economic vision, he said one of the economy's biggest requirements was genuine competition.

He said he was concerned about a Russian oligarchy made up of three main monopolistic groups in the areas of natural resources, weapons production and a small group of banks "which are close to the budget."

The banking group dealt in high-interest state treasury bills, or GKOs, that once bore a 650 percent annual interest rate, nearly triple inflation, and now are running about double inflation, which he pegged at about 20 percent.
These high rates of return effectively discouraged other business investment, he said.

"Listen who is going to invest, who is going to do anything in industries (when) you have 40 percent (interest)," he asked. "You would have two percent a year if that would be successful, in three years or something."
"It's a major disincentive," he said. "It's much easier to buy and sell these bonds."
